newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits five-month low vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits five-month low vs yen.

text.p: The dollar tumbled to the lowest level against the yen in five months on Tuesday as speculation that Japan would raise interest rates sparked large selling of the greenback.
Higher Japanese rates would make yen-based assets more attractive, drawing away funds from U.S. investments.

The dollar had fallen in European trading to 111.98 yen, its lowest level since December 1996 on reports that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party was considering making a recommendation to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan raise its official discount rate.
The Bank of Japan has kept its official discount rate at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995.

"As long as that fear is out there, that's going to keep being traded off even though it may never come to fruition any time soon," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis in North America at MMS International. "Fears move markets."
The dollar bounced from the lows and stood above 113 yen after Japanese officials warned that the yen's rise had been too rapid and a rate hike was not likely in the short-term.
The dollar remains anaemic, however, after having lost near 11 percent from 4-1/2 year peaks of 127.46 yen on May 1.
At about 10:40 a.m. EST 1440 GMT, the dollar fetched 113.56 yen, vs 115.75 yen late Monday. The dollar also fell sharply to 1.6945 German marks from 1.7080 marks.

Reverberations from news of a huge rise in Japan's trade surplus also continued to ripple through currency markets. Japan's trade surplus more than doubled in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday that the rise in the surplus was temporary and unlikely to become a major issue with other countries.

Still, Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York, emphasised that the important point is that Mitsuzuka admitted Japan's surplus was increasing. "So, that's why the market reacted by selling the dollar against yen," Igarashi said.
Dealers also noted rumours that funds of billionaire financier George Soros were selling dollars for yen.
Analysts said the dollar may not regain its recent highs even if the U.S. Federal Reserve raises interest rates at its policy-making meeting on Tuesday.
The Fed raised the federal funds rate -- the rate banks charge each other for short-term loans -- by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent after its last meeting in March.

"The trend is very strongly pro-yen at the moment. And I suspect the dollar will come under pressure even if the Fed raises interest rates this evening," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.

"For a long time, dollar/yen has been out of control. We had an unbalanced market, we had huge skew in positioning. Everyone was short of yen. It was the trade of last year: borrow yen -- sell it. That was an unsustainable situation and it is being reversed," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4060 Swiss francs from 1.4265 and edged up to Canadian $1.3723 from C$1.3713. Sterling rose to $1.6465 from $1.6400.
